leads.title: Show HN: PatchWave - Add static analysis and automerge to Dependabot
leads.description: Hey Hacker News, we're Ben, Josh, and Donnie, co-founders of PatchWave. PatchWave is a GitHub App that combines static analysis and eval'ed agents to analyze and (optionally) auto-merge PRs it deems as safe. If a Dependabot PR breaks your CI build, a fix agent works to get CI passing again. Dependabot PRs suck. Nobody likes dealing with them. Most of the time they go ignored or a senior engineer spends their valuable time dealing with them. Before PatchWave, I ran a freelance business charging clients hourly to do exactly this kind of "keep the lights on" work. Even at our small startup, we'd spend Monday mornings dealing with Dependabot PRs. Having a human-in-the-loop working with an agent on these PRs was time consuming and, often, agents would get lazy and not actually validate how an upstream change affected the codebase. And, as the quantity and severity of CVEs increases, merging security updates quickly becomes increasingly important. PatchWave is a set of specialized agents that uses static analysis tools on context we gather deterministically. 1. We pull the changelog, the code diff between versions, security advisories, and CI results. 2. The agent checks out your code in an isolated sandbox, where it uses structural code search, type checkers and your project's own toolchain to understand how your codebase uses each dependency being updated. Every Dependabot PR gets a report. You can see a few examples (against OSS repos) here: https://reports.patchwave.ai/alam00000/bentopdf/pull/913 and https://reports.patchwave.ai/shipshapecode/shepherd/pull/355... 3. If CI fails, we automatically dispatch a fix agent to try to get CI green again. For most PRs, this means updating your code to use a newer API, fixing linting/formatting issues, etc. 4. We have an optional feature that allows auto-merging certain PRs when PatchWave deems them as safe and the PR aligns with your auto-merge policy. Our recommended auto-merge policy is to auto-merge patch/minor/major dev dependencies and patch/minor production dependencies. You can customize this policy or turn auto-merge off entirely. PatchWave will skip auto-merge in a bunch of cases where a human should review. For instance, if provenance changes (e.g., a package that's usually published by GitHub Actions via Trusted Publishing is suddenly published by an API Key), we require human review before merging. Dependabot also instituted an on-by-default 3-day cooldown to reduce the risk of supply chain attacks. If PatchWave makes any changes via a fix agent, we'll always require your review before merge. Currently, PatchWave only works with Dependabot and GitHub. We plan to offer Renovate support in the future. We've eval'ed the agents the most against TypeScript and Ruby, but are always adding to our eval suite to improve accuracy. The fix agent works best with PRs that require modest code changes. For large updates, especially updates that span multiple majors, our fix agent will give up and provide you a remediation plan to help you mitigate. On the privacy/security side of the house, our SOC 2 Type II audit is in progress (see trust.contextbridge.ai). We only run on repos you select, our agents run in a short-lived microVM per run, we use Amazon Bedrock with zero-data-retention, and never train on your code. We're offering 25 free PRs per GitHub org, per month with no credit card required. Additional PRs are billed at about $1/PR, with discounts for higher volume. We also would love to accelerate OSS projects, so reach out to ask about additional free credits. If you hate dealing with Dependabot PRs, we'd love for you to give it a shot and tell us what you think. Josh, Donnie, and I will be around answering any questions and responding to any feedback you have.

leads.title: Ask HN: Techniques for productive AI use in the workspace
leads.description: Hey HN, Like so many other SWEs right now, I am trying to find ways to enhance my development experience without taking away from the quality of my work or the things I find enjoyable about software engineering, especially as one who very much enjoys the act of pulling something together using well crafted code. leads.title: Recruiters told me AI screening overlooks the best candidates. True?
leads.description: After submitting a lot of CVs recently, I’ve separately been asking recruiters and hiring managers, in-house and agency, how they’re coping now that applications can be written, enhanced or fabricated by AI, and graded by AI. An in-house recruiter at a 2,000-person company said their ranking tool grades CVs A to D, and the people they end up hiring are frequently the C’s. An agency director trialled fully automated screeners and said they “overlooked some of the strongest candidates”. A hiring manager, after a run of fabricated applications, built their own grader and auto-rejects anyone who matches the job spec too closely, on the basis that no real candidate meets 100% of the requirements. I’ve seen a few similar posts along the lines of “I’d probably be rejected applying for my own job”. Everyone said most CVs now have AI involvement, many are the job spec fed back as experience, and the truth only comes out on the screening call. If you hire engineers or any other role: has the CV stopped carrying signal for you, and what are you using instead? If AI screening is actually working for you, which tool and how? I’d like the counter-examples as much as the confirmations.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python wire client rejects valid responses larger than 16 KiB (e.g., LBS GET with block size > 16360)
leads.description:
## Python wire client rejects valid responses larger than 16 KiB (e.g., LBS GET with block size > 16360)

At `3de151b` (`master`), `tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py` defines

    MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES = 16384

with the comment "This is a somewhat arbitrary value", and `Wire.send_recv()` reads the whole response with a single bounded call:

    idnum, record = split_packet(self.sock.recv(MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES))

`split_packet()` then requires the *entire* frame inside that one buffer:

    record, crc = struct.unpack_from('>%dsI' % record_length, packet, offset=16)
    assert len(packet) == len(record) + 16 + 4

A Wire frame for a record of length `N` is `N + 20` bytes, so any response record longer than 16364 bytes cannot be processed: `recv()` returns at most 16384 bytes and `struct.unpack_from` raises `struct.error`.

This is separate from #358 (responses fragmented across reads of a small packet). PR #359's stated fix explicitly keeps "the existing total response-size limit", so this bug remains even after #359 is merged.

### Valid server responses that exceed the cap

1. **LBS GET with block size > 16360.** The block size is operator-configured via `lbs -b`, validated to `[PROTO_LBS_BLKLEN_MIN, PROTO_LBS_BLKLEN_MAX]` = `[512, 131072]` (`lbs/main.c`, `lib/proto_lbs/proto_lbs.h`). An LBS GET response record is `4 (status) + blklen` bytes (`lib/proto_lbs/proto_lbs_server.c`, `proto_lbs_response_get()`). Any deployment configured with block size ≥ 16361 — legal up to the documented maximum of 131072 — produces GET responses the Python client cannot read. The C server imposes no such limit: `proto_lbs_request_parse()` `malloc()`s APPEND payloads dynamically and `wire_writepacket_getbuf()` sizes GET responses to the configured block size.

2. **KVLDS RANGE responses.** The response record grows with the data returned: `4 (status) + 4 (num_pairs) + nextkey + Σ(1+keylen + 1+valen)` (each pair up to 514 bytes). For 100-byte keys/values, a range response with roughly 80 pairs already exceeds the cap; `tests/python/dump_kvlds.py` requests `maxsize = 8192` pairs per range call, so the dump tool fails on most non-trivial datasets. The C-side range response is likewise dynamically sized.

### Reproduction (real C server, no mocks)

On `3de151b`, with `crcmod` installed:

    $ ./lbs/lbs -s /tmp/repro/lbs.sock -d /tmp/repro/storage -b 32768 -1 &
    $ python3 - <<'EOF'
    import sys
    sys.path.insert(0, 'tests/python')
    from kivaloo import proto_lbs
    p = proto_lbs.Proto_lbs('/tmp/repro/lbs.sock')
    print("params():", p.params())
    data = bytes(range(256)) * 128          # one 32 KiB block
    print("append():", p.append(1, 0, data))
    print("get():", p.get(0))
    EOF

    params(): (32768, 0)
    append(): 0 1
    get() FAILED -> error: unpack_from requires a buffer of at least 32792 bytes
        for unpacking 32776 bytes at offset 16 (actual buffer size is 16384)

The C `lbs` server accepts the 32 KiB block and serves it (no server-side error); only the Python client fails.

### Impact

- The Python client cannot interoperate with any LBS deployment configured with block size > 16360 (legal up to 131072).
- `dump_kvlds.py` and any KVLDS RANGE consumer fail once a range response exceeds 16 KiB.
- The test suite cannot exercise the C server with non-default (larger) block sizes, because the harness itself rejects the responses.

### Suggested fix

In `send_recv()`: read the 16-byte header first (as #359 proposes), then read exactly `record_length + 4` further bytes based on the header's `record_length` field before calling `split_packet()`. This bounds the allocation by the protocol maximum (LBS: 20 + 4 + 131072 = 131096 bytes; KVLDS: bounded by the requested data) instead of a fixed 16384. `MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` can then be removed or raised to the protocol maximum.

### Scope / disclosure

This report is limited to the Python client/helper and its callers (`tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py`). I am not reporting a crash in the C storage server, a security exploit, or stored-data corruption. The C client (`lib/wire/wire_readpacket.c`) reads complete packets and is unaffected.

This report, investigation and reproduction were prepared by an LLM with the authorization of the `zhangb06` account owner. I am available to discuss the problem or a fix through this account. No live customer data, external service testing, or payment credentials were used.

leads.title: Programmer owns the architecture, AI implements crate-level modules in Rust — how does this compare to other languages?
leads.description: After working on several Rust projects with AI assistance, I want to share a division of responsibility that has worked well in practice, and ask whether others have found the same — or a better approach in other languages. The core model: The programmer owns the world-view of the project — module boundaries, crate structure, system architecture, and design trade-offs. The AI implements the flesh — concrete trait implementations, error handling, boilerplate, and module-level logic. The programmer owns the architecture; the AI owns the implementation. And the Rust compiler makes sure the two stay honest with each other. In practice, I have found that AI can already generate crate-level Rust code that compiles, runs correctly, and is architecturally sound — requiring only minor adjustments. Occasionally it produces solutions I would not have thought of myself. Why Rust works particularly well for this model: The borrow checker and type system act as a verification layer between the programmer's intent and the AI's output. If the AI misunderstands the architecture, the compiler rejects it. This means the programmer does not need to read every line of generated code — the compiler enforces the contract. This is not just about safety. It also forces the AI to produce code that is structurally honest. There is no way to paper over a bad design with runtime workarounds. Comparison with other languages: Python — The iteration cycle is fastest, and AI generates idiomatic Python reliably. But there is no compiler to catch architectural mismatches. The programmer must read and verify far more of the generated code manually. The division of responsibility is blurry. TypeScript — Static types help, and strict mode catches a meaningful class of AI mistakes. A reasonable middle ground, though AI frequently reaches for any to silence errors, weakening the contract. Go — Simple syntax reduces the surface area for AI mistakes. But nil pointer panics and verbose error handling mean AI output still requires careful review. The compiler helps less than Rust. Java — Mature static analysis tooling provides a review pipeline, but AI tends to generate verbose, over-engineered boilerplate. The null problem remains. Architecturally, the programmer ends up doing more correction work. C++ — AI can generate C++ that compiles but contains subtle memory bugs the compiler does not catch. The division of responsibility breaks down — the programmer must verify deeply, which defeats the purpose. Personal note: I came to Rust from a Java background, after also working with Go, JavaScript, Python, and C++. It took three attempts and roughly six months of serious effort before Rust clicked. What surprised me was that Rust is, in a deeper sense, a remarkably clean language. The complexity is front-loaded — concentrated at compile time — so the resulting code is predictable and self-consistent in a way that Java or C++ rarely achieves at scale. In the AGI era, that front-loaded strictness turns out to be exactly what you want when working with AI. The compiler becomes a shared contract between the programmer's world-view and the AI's implementation. Neither side can cheat. Question: Is this division of responsibility — programmer as architect, AI as implementer — viable in your experience? And does the language choice fundamentally change how well this model works? If you could only choose one language for AI-assisted development going forward, which would it be — and why?

leads.title: Show HN: Pointless but mostly-exact clone of Hacker News
leads.description: Source code: http://github.com/shawwn/sharc I had more things I wanted to do with this, but I should probably admit to myself I probably won't be. The original idea was for https://news.ycombinator.lol to be "Hacker News, but all the comments are AI." Right now it's "Hacker News, but all the comments are the same as the real HN." Hence, it's completely pointless. Special thanks to dang for collaborating -- he even suggested the name for the codebase, "sharc". Development time was about four months of near daily work: https://github.com/shawwn/sharc/tree/main/docs/agents/handof... Some days I'd spend a solid 16 hours on this. What's the point? None, really. Just to test the limits of my abilities and prove to myself that I could do what pg did. It's an extremely efficient port of HN to Common Lisp. One of the project's goals was to be high performance. According to benchmarks, it can generate pages very slightly slower than real HN. (dang shared some timings on a particularly busy page, along with how many views it got over a certain time period, for benchmarking throughput. I never got around to verifying whether I can handle 24 million views a day, though, so I'd imagine something might break if you scale this up. On the other hand, I think it'll hold up.) If you're particularly offended that this is copying your comments, claim your account by going to your profile (for example, I would go to https://news.ycombinator.lol/user?id=sillysaurusx ) and then click "claim" at the bottom. It'll ask you to put a 6 digit code into your real HN profile, at which point you'll be able to reset your cloned profile's password. Log in, go to your profile page, and set "redact" to "yes", the same way you'd set "showdead" to "yes" on HN. So, why make this? Eh, call it an art project. That's code for "It would've been a lot funnier with AI generated comments, but I seem to have stopped working on this for now." I'll post an update someday, if I can figure out how to do it without paying hundreds of dollars of API token prices. /ask and /show are missing. Those were the only two features left to clone. But pretty much everything else is there. It's been running for a couple months now, so I suppose it's stable enough for a public showing. Not that there's any reason to look. Shoo! Go find a more worthy project to devote your attention to. :) Kind of melancholy admitting that I spent four months with only something pointless to show for it. But then again, here's the punchline: go to any random comment on HN, then in the url change .com to .lol and you'll see an almost pixel perfect recreation. For example, https://news.ycombinator.lol/item?id=49995615 Sadly you can't form a loop, because if you edit your original comment with a link to itself, you'd only be able to go from HN to .lol to HN. But you could list both and switch between them as much as you want. For example: https://news.ycombinator.lol/item?id=49996495 https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49996495 This project was one of the most technically demanding things I've ever done. People look at HN and go oh, that? That looks easy. If you think so, I invite you to write it yourself -- it's an exercise that'll certainly make you a better programmer, and gain appreciation for how many subtle features we enjoy here on HN. Ha, and I just discovered a new one. I mixed up the "title" and "url" boxes just now. HN popped up a nice looking overlay that said "please enter a URL", pointing to the actual url box. https://i.imgur.com/agFas7x.png The HN team is always adding something or anothe

leads.title: Show HN: Flopper is a hardware explorer for AI infrastructure and beyond
leads.description: Hello! I built Flopper to make it easier to compare GPUs and understand the tradeoffs for workloads for AI and beyond. When researching GPUs from say Nvidia, AMD, and Huawei, I kept running into the same problem: specs were scattered across datasheets, and matching them to available configurations, vendors, and prices was cumbersome and a bit weird and frankly annoyingggg! AMD made me make an account :( So I started a place to bring that information together. Flopper lets you compare GPU specs, including TDP and compute throughput in terms of flops/tops, alongside estimates for AI workloads or other compute workloads (say, ~FP32 based) I recently added pricing data from dozens of providers to help track how prices change over time. Getting reliable quotes for systems like the NVL72 is still particularly difficult tbh, not sure how I can tell you how much that costs easily due to them being behind large procurement contracts and big multi-nationals. One thing that's become fairlyyyy clear is the interest in consumer cards and local LLMs. The bigger challenge is connecting advertised specs to real-world performance. In our testing so far, I’ve seen roughly 85% of advertised throughput, but that’s a ballpark observation for the workloads I’ve tested, not a general rule and so variable (power, cooling, workload etc). I'm considering a CLI that lets people run benchmarks and submit results, potentially using MLPerf as an automation? That way, we can all compare quoted performance with the workload, configuration etc. I'd love feedback: what information is missing, how can I improve it? And what would you need to see to trust a community-submitted benchmark? Corrections and additions also very welcome - some of the measurements are best efforts (and simple multiplications) but I hope it's of some use. Thanks for looking :)

leads.title: Show HN: Privatrak – no-code, privacy-first product analytics
leads.description: Hi HN! Quick story how it started: I was a freelance web developer in the past and also worked for several companies on web applications. For some projects we didn’t have analytics at all and we had to ask ourselves too many times what our users actually use in the product. Finding a good solution was painful, since we couldn’t use a consent banner (a lot of customers from the government) and existing tools were hard to set up so nobody took the time. I started with this idea already many years ago, but only really got to develop it in the past year. So what is Privatrak? A product tracking tool which is simple to set up and doesn’t require any code for most use cases. It can be used just by tagging elements on your site in the browser. From that, funnels and analytics dashboards can be created. I also wanted to make it as easy as possible to use with AI agents, hence there is a MCP server which can be used to question the data and set up the project (every change an AI agent makes is tracked and can also easily be undone). It doesn’t store any sensitive user data and can be used without a consent banner or cookies. Sessions are calculated based on a hash that consists of the users IP address + user agent + random rotating salt (IP address and user agent are never stored) and are aggregated for each day, so the data basically only points at a group of users in the end. In many cases this is fine. Often you are only curious about a specific feature or trends and not what a specific user did. If you need to track people over multiple days or need session replays, this is not the right tool. My main goal in posting here is to get some feedback for the product. Is the daily cutoff for sessions a dealbreaker for you? I just launched it and currently only have a handful of people actually using it. I built a demo project for everybody to see how it looks without having to sign up: https://demo.privatrak.com/

leads.title: Show HN: Clawdline – Manage Claude Code/Codex sessions across computers
leads.description: I built Clawdline to manage Claude Code and Codex sessions across multiple computers in one place. It runs on multiple computers (Mac and Linux), and you can see all of your sessions in one list. Each session reports its status (working, completed, or needs attention). You can also manage all your sessions and receive notifications from your phone (web app). Herdr, T3 Code, and Orca already cover a lot of this space, and there’s overlap. When I started building Clawdline, I didn't know about Herdr, T3 Code, or Orca. So I built it to fit my own dev workflow. At first, I used Swift to build a Mac app, but I realized that it wouldn't work if I also wanted to support Linux. So I decided to rewrite it in Go. Now it can support both of them. Main Features: - Cross Machine Agent Communication: You can ask a root session ("Local") on your Mac to start a new session ("Remote") on a remote Linux machine. Once the remote session finishes its work, it notifies the root ("Local") session. - Cross Agent Communication: You can use one root session to create tasks need multiple agents. They can communicate with each other through clawdline - Scheduled Task with Webhook: You can create scheduled tasks and combine them with your service (use webhooks to trigger new agent sessions) - Board System: tasks control for Feature, Issue, Epic, Refactor, Plan - Snippet/Playbook: If there are commands you use them very often, snippet can help you - TODO: lightweight tasks - Note: Agents can leave notes to you if they need your attention - Agent Squad: assign role to any task or session - Archive: you can archive sessions and see it in one place - Others: Intelligence session naming, Image/Video display, Voice input, Machine monitor, Usage Monitor, Dev Stack Run, Deploy progress monitor... This project is open source and I have used Claude & Codex to do independent reviews on Clawdline, Herdr, T3 and Orca. (you can find the reviews on the website.) The work still needs further input and feedback. Hope this helps other developers improve their devs! :)

leads.title: Ask HN: Are Apple app reviewers sharing app ideas?
leads.description: Not accusing anyone but let me explain. I like telling stories to my kid when he goes to bed. Since there are a lot of evening doing this, I started inventing these stories and to keep it a bit interesting I started asking him about what or how would he change the outcomes, and then it struck me. What if I create stories where readers can interact and change the outcomes. So for the past year I was working on this game engine that would allow to create stories and defined rules, game mechanics per game, and allow players to pick their own route through the story. I finished the app and wrote a couple of stories and registered the app on the App Store. At that point (more then 3 months ago) there was no other app with that name. In that period I sent it up for review, which took a more then week every time, and it was rejected 3 times for the stupid reasons: - in app image text not visible: I used a small cover image from stories, and one of them had this text on a wall in the background - they've said text unreadable - I picked the secondary category for the app as books: I thought that games would be a good fit for the main category, why not pick books for the second - well this was not right again - When I selected the App Store countries I also selected China: they've said that books are only allowed to be published in China if I register as book published there - so I had to remove it from that store, although they said I cannot pick books as my secondary category After all 3 reviews, which each of them took me around 10 minutes to fix and re-request another approval check, took weeks in-between. The last and final one took 1 whole month, and this after requesting an expedited review 3 times, because no body would answer the feedback dev-reviewer board. Anyway, I was so happy when yesterday my app got finally approved and it landed on the store. So as anyone would do, I picked up my phone and searched for it. And yeah, it was there, but there was another app with the same name, same idea, same everything (almost). My happiness immediately faded, and I was so disappointed in me, that I did not see it before, but then I got angry. I immediately checked the "What's new" section of this app, just to find out that it was just published, like 2 weeks ago (suspicious). I then went into this developer's account to see their other apps, and to my astonishment, they are all copied apps, and all of them first released 2 weeks ago. I search all these apps, and yes there's another app with those same names. And then it struck me, could it be that I got delayed for a whole month, while somebody just copied my idea, or other devs ideas while they wait and cannot do anything about it, just to find out they've came second. With AI being so fast, you cannot compete any more with it. You can nowadays recreate apps in just hours, while the original dev might have needed months, or years to reach the same point. Bottom line is, that I do not point fingers, but my experience raised some doubts in my mind. Just wanted to share this with you and to ask if anyone had this in the past?

I love solving problems, it's part of me. I know it has got a lot harder to land a development gig but I've worked with modern stuff like AI-generated briefs for meetings, bug logs automatically sent emails to responsible developers, at a point I had an Agent dedicated to verifying how well our code was written so I feel like I've kept up with the innovations, and skills. But I have no idea how to land a job in software development anymore: nothing seems enough. I have tried for over a year and the only reason I can withstand this much waiting while seeking a job in that field is because of my exceptional employment history (including working to Silicon Valley companies), but it has got to a point I am worried. I've asked my friends who are also developers and they feel similarly, we do not know where to dedicate our effors, as if the competency of software engineers were transformed irrelevant because of AI. We know what happened, we just don't know what to do with all the competency we embody. I've taken a liking to working as a bartender in my local city, because that's kind of the only job I can land lately, but as soon as my degree in Computer Engineering is mentioned I'm set aside as a anti-social computer expert who will never take a low-paying job like "this". (Secretly I found it very fun, fullfilling in a way I never thought I needed because money was my priority at the beggining of the carreer) How the hell do we transform this competency and learning ability of software engineers into desireable company-adding value skills? (I swear this is not generated by AI, I don't even know how to prove anymore)

Show HN: What a major earthquake does to Vancouver
leads.description: About 10 years ago, I attended a presentation by someone who had compiled existing engineering reports to describe the impact of a major earthquake on infrastructure in British Columbia. It was really striking, and it has stayed in the back of my mind ever since. I am now the point of contact for downtown Vancouver in the French community's emergency network, and it drives me nuts that most people I talk to have no emergency kit at home and basically no water. People are shocked, or in denial, when I mention that it could take weeks to restore electricity and that they will have to rely on their own food and water for at least several days. So I decided to build a public-facing site that compiles existing information, as a way to lay out the facts and help convince people, instead of hearing back that "the army will come" or that "there are emergency food reserves" (there aren't). I see this as a citizen initiative, with one main message: go buy some water and canned food, it's your civic duty. I relied on AI agents to compile the information, which is spread across hundreds of reports. With different levels of validation, plus my own review, I am confident the information is reliable, even if some details may not be fully up to date. The process took 2–3 weeks, alongside work, a toddler and a baby! I'm posting it here because: 1) I'm curious to get feedback and suggestions. 2) Many HN readers are on the West Coast or in other seismic areas, so even if you're not in Vancouver, the general recommendations may be of interest. Be smart: buy some food and water. Cheers Thomas

leads.title: Show HN: Use your own Amazon SES account for email workflows
leads.description: Hey HN! We built SendOps because we think email can be a good medium to help users through their journey with your product. Onboarding a new user and helping them in their journey in your product can be specific to the actions they take, their goals and it allows them to read or explore in their own time and not based on your timeline. After a while of running a service for a few years, we all end up with a few thousand if not hundreds of thousands of emails who signed up for our service. Some become customers, some never try the service and some might activate at some point in the future, when the time is right. Email workflows (drip campaigns etc) have existed for a long time. However, all workflow providers charge both per email and per contact you have on your books. This usually means one of two things: 1. you pay a lot of money for contacts you don't email often. 2. you have to keep modifying your list based on your communication to avoid higher bills. We also wanted to be able to build effective and useful email workflows using our coding agents. The result of our work is SendOps: SendOps is an email workflow product that sends emails through your own AWS SES account, charges no fees for contacts, or per email (just a flat fee subscription) and lets your coding agents help you with building your email workflows. We hope you find SendOps useful. We've been members of HN community for a long time and love how direct and helpful your feedback is. So, please try it out if you think it can be useful to you (we have free-forever tier) and let us know what you think! https://sendops.dev Thank you

leads.title: "Wrong" Email
leads.description: Let’s say your LinkedIn account has been restricted, and you can no longer access it. You might try to visit: https://www.linkedin.com//help/linkedin/ask/sdsupport or https://www.linkedin.com//help/linkedin/ask/ppq to contact customer support. You fill out the form and click "Submit," but for a split second, a pop-up appears: "we`re sorry. There was an error creating your case. Please try again" and than redirect. You might try switching browsers, using private/incognito mode, changing devices (desktop, phone), or even using a different IP address—but nothing works. You keep encountering the same error. However, as soon as you change the email address to one not associated with the restricted account, the form submits successfully. This proves, beyond a doubt, that the "error" was linked solely to the email address; changing the email—while keeping everything else the same—changes the outcome. Okay, so you’ve submitted the request—what happens next? You receive a response (here are some excerpts; the exact wording may vary slightly): "You are contacting us from an email address that differs from the one registered to your account." "An account restriction should not, in itself, prevent you from contacting us via the provided form." "To protect privacy, I cannot, without a direct request from the account owner sent from their registered email address, do the following:" "Therefore, please reach out to us using the form mentioned above, ensuring you use the email address registered to your account. This will allow us to proceed with reviewing your inquiry and provide the necessary assistance." Brilliant. In other words, LinkedIn blocks support requests made using the email address linked to a restricted account—yet when they receive a request made (out of necessity) from a different email address, they close the ticket and instruct you to submit a new one using the "correct" email—which is technically impossible to do. And they are flat-out lying—let me repeat: An account restriction should not, in itself, prevent you from contacting us via the provided form. Even if you explicitly point out this situation in your request—and even suggest that they email you directly at the address linked to your account (which they do very, very rarely—maybe once in every 50 attempts)—they still respond with that same template. This raises two questions: 1. Are the LinkedIn support staff genuinely unaware of this, even though they ought to know? Or do they know, but are lying and moking with users on purpose? I, for one, have never been able to figure this out. 2. Why is so little known about this, given that the situation has persisted for years and has been documented many times ( as example https://youtu.be/RRIm1ReQ_6A?t=221 (t=180) ) ? And why is there no reaction to it? It’s as if it’s been tacitly accepted.

leads.title: Ask HN: What happened to our collective ethos?
leads.description: I’m an outsider to both Silicon Valley and enterprise IT; I’m just a freelance consultant and web host plying my trade in the suburbs of Charlotte. But I have generally presumed that we all share a common nostalgic ideal rooted in the memories and stories of Bell Labs, Xerox PARC, and their unbound, open-ended exploration of science, technology, and the limits of their imaginations. I’ve been told that the economic and regulatory conditions that allowed these monuments to human endeavor ultimately shifted, monopolies were broken up, assets were sold off, and it ultimately served as the incubator for the modern technology industry. But we’ve since seen companies emerge with market dominance and wealth that the Bell Group could only dream about, who presided over a decade and a half of near-zero interest rates. None of whom elected to establish/fund public-facing research campuses stuffed with Nobel laureates conducting their own frontier research departments. What’s worse, most of them instead chose to turn their oligopolies towards seeking to control the media and political process, privatizing what was left of America’s public aerospace programs, gatekeeping research and development, and subsidizing their further encroachments with the resulting government contracts. How are these the people we granted so much power and influence to? Was it simply that Silicon Valley was captured by the financial industry? Was the origin story always a convenient myth, that nobody ever actually took seriously, or objected to when it was cynically exploited by the patently disingenuous and greedy CEOs who have, without exception, acted in the worst interests of their users, society, and the planet? Just the base selfishness of human nature? Were the research and development labs of the post-war American era just a flash in the pan, or could Silicon Valley someday rediscover its lost soul? I’d reckon we’d all be better off for it, but I am also concerned that I simply fell the for the marketing hype, and there never was the altruistic spirit of innovation I’d always imagined.

leads.title: Show HN: git-dupe – Version private files alongside a public Git repo
leads.description: Hi HN! I made git-dupe to solve the problem where I have notes, skills, and agent instructions that are part of my personal workflow, so I do not want them committed to the public repo, but at the same time, I want them to be in the project at the correct locations (e.g., AGENTS.md file locations matter), and these files cannot be simply gitignored because I want versioning for them. The solution that I've come upon is versioning those agent files in another repo, say <private-repo> (this repo is private to me and holds the history for my agent files). The project itself is open to the public in another <public-repo>. I overlap the two repos to solve the problem (i.e., they share the same worktree). $ git status --short # the public repo ?? AGENTS.md ?? notes/ $ git dupe init # the private repo Initialized empty Git repository in /home/brian/code/project/.git/dupe/ $ git dupe add notes/ AGENTS.md # the private repo hint: notes is now hidden from the project's Git; run from the root, 'git dupe unhide -- notes' stops hiding it $ git dupe commit -m "Notes and agent instructions" # the private repo [main (root-commit) 3eb3af9] Notes and agent instructions 3 files changed, 3 insertions(+) create mode 100644 .gitdupe create mode 100644 AGENTS.md create mode 100644 notes/todo.md $ git status --short # the public repo: nothing $ git dupe log --oneline # the private repo: your files 3eb3af9 Notes and agent instructions In short, git-dupe allows two Git repos to share the same worktree, while using native Git for most operations. Most git-dupe commands behave just like normal Git commands, operating on the private repo instead. git-dupe currently supports Linux and macOS, and is under the MIT License; the git-dupe repo contains much more extensive technical documentation documentation for those who are interested. If you have any feedback/questions about git-dupe, feel free to message. I hope it helps! Fun fact: the git-dupe project itself is using git-dupe for versioning.

Sweep the GRPO learning rate: 5e-7 may be too low to move the policy
leads.description:
`configs/grpo.yaml` sets `learning_rate: 5e-7`. FEEDBACK.md Problem 4: published GRPO-on-LoRA work sits between 1e-6 and 1e-5, and `kl_coef: 0.1` already provides regularization, so there is room. At 5e-7 with this corpus size, three epochs is very few gradient updates and the policy may simply not move enough to measure.

**What to do**

1. Run the baseline in #7 at 5e-7 first, so there is a reference.
2. Sweep 2e-6 and 5e-6, everything else held constant, 3 epochs each.
3. Compare per-epoch mean reward. FEEDBACK.md gives the reading: steady improvement of 0.02 to 0.05 per epoch is healthy, under 0.01 per epoch means the LR is too low, unstable or collapsing means too high.
4. Judge the winner with the judge classifier and the LLM judge, never with the reward classifier.

**Order matters:** run #18 first. If group reward std is near zero, no learning rate will help and the sweep would attribute a reward-design problem to the optimizer.

leads.title: The reward analysis backlog is blocked on a GRPO run that has never happened
leads.description:
`outputs/` contains `classifier/` only: `best`, `final`, `judge`, `sanity_probe.json`, `backbone_comparison.json`. There is no `outputs/grpo/`, no `outputs/eval/`, and no completions anywhere in the repo. PLAN.md Steps 4 through 7 are untouched. GRPO has never run.

Meanwhile, four open issues all ask questions that can only be answered by reading completions from a GRPO run:

- #30 is the completion length distribution pinned at `max_completion_length`
- #15 reward-hacking audit of the top-k completions
- #18 group reward variance, near-zero spread means no gradient
- #19 learning rate sweep, 5e-7 may be too low to move the policy

Three separate contributors have now written analysis tooling against this gap. #31 (`audit_rewards.py`, closed by its author) and #33 (`analyze_completion_lengths.py`, open) are both instruments for data that does not exist, and both PR descriptions say so in their own words: "the actual histogram data needs completions from a real GRPO training", "the tool is unexercised on real data".

That is not the contributors' fault. The issues read as if the data were sitting there. But the effect is that effort keeps flowing into measuring a run nobody has launched, and none of the four issues can close.

**The actual order**

1. **#12 first, and it is the only issue labelled `blocking` for a reason.** The classifier has never seen a base-model generation, which is the entire distribution it will score during GRPO. Every reward the policy receives passes through it. Running Step 5 before fixing #12 produces a run whose rewards are untrustworthy, which means the #30 and #15 analyses would be measuring an artifact.
2. **Then Step 5, GRPO from base**, producing `outputs/grpo/` and an `outputs/eval/latest.json` written with `--reward-config` so the per-prompt reward breakdowns exist. Without that flag the breakdown keys are absent (`scripts/evaluate.py:173`) and the audit tooling has nothing to read.
3. **Then #30, #15, #18, #19**, in whatever order the run's numbers make interesting.

**What to do here**

Make the dependency explicit so contributors are not drawn into building instruments for absent data:

- Note on #30, #15, #18 and #19 that they are gated on a Step 5 run, and that until then only the tool can be delivered, not the finding.
- Consider a `blocked` label, or milestones, so the gating is visible from the issue list rather than only from reading `outputs/`.
- Once the run exists, post the artifact paths on each of the four issues so the tooling has a concrete target.

The project is not short on tooling. It is short on one run.

leads.title: Addressing EU Cyber Resilience Act
leads.description: By Jacob Mammoliti, Solutions Architect, RapidFort The EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) is a regulation (EU 2024/2847) that defines mandatory cybersecurity requirements for all products with digital elements sold in EU markets. Reporting obligations began on Sept. 11, with full enforcement commencing on Dec. 11, 2027. The CRA sets new requirements for teams working with containers and Kubernetes that impact how cloud native applications are built, distributed, and maintained throughout their lifecycle. Cloud Native Environments and CRA Scope Regardless of where a distributing organization is located, the CRA covers all container images, Kubernetes operators, and Helm charts with commercial support that are available to EU customers. The regulation specifies its scope as “products with digital elements” available in EU markets, and that also includes a lot of the cloud native stack. CRA scope covers container images distributed publicly, commercial Kubernetes operators, open source with commercial backing, and Helm charts with commercial support. Open-source projects may also be impacted, including those with commercial backing or support contracts. In addition, the regulation requires a compliance chain throughout the cloud native supply chain. CRA Requirements for Container Teams The CRA introduces requirements that directly impact how teams build and operate container infrastructure. These categories include: Vulnerability Management – SBOM data, continuous monitoring, and 24-hour ENISA reporting for exploited vulnerabilities. Security by Design and Default – Hardened base images, minimal attack surfaces, and secure defaults as regulatory requirements. Long-Term Security (5+ Years) – Ongoing security updates, rebuild pipelines, and backward-compatible patching for product lifetime. This Act specifies that base images must be hardened with unnecessary components eliminated and secure configurations applied before products are made available on the market. The regulation orders what many in the cloud native community have long wanted – now minimal attack surfaces and secure defaults are regulatory requirements rather than recommendations. As a result of the CRA, organizations must maintain Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) data, continuously monitor for vulnerabilities, and remediate within defined timeframes. Under the Act’s Article 14, actively exploited vulnerabilities must result in an early warning to The European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (maintaining the acronym from the agency’s previous name European Network and Information Security Agency – ENISA) within 24 hours of discovery, followed by a full notification within 72 hours. This mandates that organizations’ detection and incident response processes need to operate at scale across clusters. Now products require security updates for a minimum of five years from the date of being available on the market, or throughout the expected product lifetime if that period is shorter, as stated in Article 13 of the CRA. For container teams, this requires tracking container versions deployed in customer environments, ensuring backward compatibility, and maintaining rebuild pipelines for older images – all while addressing security issues discovered years after release.

leads.title: Ask HN: A plea to help me help my father
leads.description: My mother died in a car accident yesterday. To my great regret, I had constantly been putting off seeing her for years, and it leaves me deeply stricken that not only did she die with nobody at her side, but that she had spent years alone, with nobody keeping her company as she became isolated in older age. While delivering the news, my father told me his doctor had given him two years to live, ten months ago. I don't want to repeat the same mistake. I want to spend the next year with him, fulfilling his dream of a cross-country road trip, something which he gave up on to raise me as a single father. However, I cannot afford to do this. I did odd jobs here and there, but the kind of small-time contract work I dabbled in has dried up with the advent of LLMs, and my own savings are insufficient. I would be incredibly grateful to be given a job opportunity with remote, flexible hours that would allow me to work while fulfilling my father's dream. I am not a conventional hire. I didn't finish high school, I don't have a formal employment history. I can offer a portfolio of personal projects but my resume is the kind that gets auto-rejected. I can be incredibly useful, if you'll give someone the system overlooks a chance. I've spent 12+ hours a day for years programming all kinds of random things, most with no market value but which have developed my skills tremendously. I have experience with just about anything you can name, from embedded assembly and bare metal devops to Android apps and web dev and everything in between. On the off chance I don't, I'll learn anything you can throw at me. I simply love programming for programming's sake. I can wrangle a chatbot if that's what the job demands, but I prefer to use them for research and brainstorming and hand roll the best code I can myself, delivering something of far higher quality than you can get with prompting. I have confidence in my own skills and that I can eventually break into the market on my own merits. But I don't have 'eventually'. My mother is dead and my father is dying. It's my own fault things ended up this way, not being the child I should have been for them earlier, and these regrets are mine to bear, but all I can do is ask for help to prevent another regret being added to the pile. I promise I will make it worth your while if you can give me a chance. (A contact e-mail address is in the profile. Please forgive the anonymous account, it shames me to be begging like this... )

leads.title: Show HN: Correct Hooks – Easy webhook auth with asymmetric signatures
leads.description: A while back, I needed to make a webhook system for a project I was working on. I pretty quickly found out that webhook auth is not an entirely solved problem with people frequently implementing DIY solutions. I also found out that while using some form of asymmetric signature (eg. oauth tokens) is common with regular api auth, most webhook producers use symmetric signatures (HMAC) instead. This bugged the hell out of me because the webhook functionality I needed was pretty basic, but using symmetric signatures, which requires the webhook producer to hold onto a secret for every endpoint they send webhooks to, introduced a major secret management problem. Designing and implementing novel secret management techniques for my web app felt like a bad idea, so I started looking into why so many people use symmetric signatures instead of asymmetric signatures. I frequently saw performance listed as a problem with asymmetric signatures, so I thought this might be why they weren't more broadly used, but a quick benchmark proved that wrong (HMAC signing is much faster, but ed25519 is still fast enough that it doesn't matter). It seemed like the biggest barrier to using asymmetric signatures was added development complexity. There are small but important details that need to be included in an asymmetric signature, getting asymmetric keys into the right format is more complicated than for symmetric keys, and the crypto libraries you're working with can have sharp edges. That complexity makes it more difficult for a webhook producer to implement (and document) asymmetric signatures, but then all of their consumers also have to implement the verification step (hopefully correctly). Building a library that does these steps for you is difficult because it has to be available in any language a webhook consumer might be using, not just the language the webhook producer uses. But it kept bugging me that we're all using a less good form of authentication just because we haven't packaged up the steps to sign and verify an asymmetric signature that is secure for webhooks, so now I've built that library. With a few language implementations to serve as a template, replicating this in enough languages that the large majority of developers can use it feels totally doable, and I am hoping to get several more languages implemented over the next few weeks.

leads.title: [CRITICAL] R0's citation collapse is reward-optimal, not emergent hacking: reframe it
leads.description:
**Severity:** critical · **Raised by reviewer(s):** A, B, C

**Location:** ch3 §3.3–3.4 (R0 definition); ch4 §4.4–4.5; ch5 §5.1; abstract

### Problem
Under R0 every weight except EM is 0, but invalid episodes still get `PROTOCOL_REWARD = -1.0` (`src/needle/training/rollouts.py:37`). A citation to an unknown title or sentence raises `SearchEnvironmentError` (`src/needle/environment/search.py:170-180`), which makes the episode invalid. An uncited answer is valid and can earn +1. So under R0 a citation can only cost reward and never earn any, and dropping citations is the reward-maximising policy. B0's main failure mode was exactly this: 85/130 failures were invented citations. The thesis presents the collapse as reward hacking (Skalse) and concludes that "the shortcut comes from the reward", which is close to true by construction.

### Why it matters
Every reviewer flagged this independently. An examiner will say the headline RQ2 finding is a designed-in incentive.

### Suggested fix
- Add a short derivation in §3.4 and §4.5: under R0, E[R | cite] ≤ E[R | no cite].
- Reframe as "outcome reward + citation-validity penalty pushes the policy to omit citations". The interesting part becomes *timing and seed-dependence* (s7 did not collapse).
- From R0 s8/s9 `metrics.jsonl` rollouts, count the share of invalid rollouts caused by citation errors in steps 1–96 (CPU only).
- List as future work an R0 variant that requires citing but only checks the format.

---
_From the simulated IEEE peer review of the thesis (3 independent reviewers, merged). Tracked in the summary issue._

leads.title: [MAJOR] Analyse VEGR term weighting and report coverage weakness up front
leads.description:
**Severity:** major · **Raised by reviewer(s):** B, C

**Location:** `src/needle/rewards/__init__.py:23-29, 182-194`; abstract; Table 4.1

### Problem
Evidence and retrieval terms supply up to 3 of VEGR's ~5 points. A wrong answer citing gold sentences can score high: the first R0 s7 episode has EM 0 and a VEGR total of 2.87. VEGR coverage (0.473 / 0.513 / 0.333) is *below* untrained B0 (0.472) on 2 of 3 seeds, but the abstract only highlights precision of 0.73–0.75.

### Why it matters
This is selective reporting, and the weighting may explain why EM doesn't move between R0 and R1.

### Suggested fix
- From existing rollouts, report each term's share of within-group reward variance and the fraction of high-reward rollouts with EM = 0 (CPU).
- State in the abstract that VEGR does not raise coverage, and pair this with the R3 trade-off.

---
_From the simulated IEEE peer review of the thesis (3 independent reviewers, merged). Tracked in the summary issue._

If you'd like to try it, head to https://whitehirst.com and fill out the contact form and I'll pick a handful to get started with. leads.title: Tell HN: I unknowingly broke the PHP RCE embargo. I am sorry
leads.description: I posted here about the then-upcoming PHP RCEs related to CVE-2026-109618 & CVE-2026-109619. I appreciate this has had considerable knock-on effects with the schedule for co-ordinated disclosure, and created additional workload. I am truly sorry. I take full responsibility for my actions. It was not remotely my intention to cause any of the subsequent side effects. At the time of posting, I didn't know about any embargo. My contact had told me there was no embargo, and her contact had told her the same thing. As someone who follows the 4-weekly PHP release cycle and compiles it from source, my intention was to alert others in a similar position to be aware of the importance/urgency of the updates. That clearly backfired in a pretty wild fashion. I have learned my lesson.

leads.title: Chinese Universities in Jiangsu Begin Paying Staff in Digital Yuan
Tell HN: I've been paying for a rural Tanzanian's education for 10 years
leads.description: Ten years ago I was 19 and traveling through East Africa, and I spent a summer in Ibumila, a village in the Njombe highlands of Tanzania. There's no school in the village. The nearest one is a boarding school an hour away that costs a few hundred dollars a year, which is out of reach for most families there and was about two weeks of summer job money for me. The daughter of the family I stayed with, Anwarite, was 11. I offered to pay her fees and told myself I'd keep paying as long as she wanted to keep going. This summer she graduated from the University of Dar es Salaam with a degree in Language Studies, and last week she told me she'd been accepted into a Master of Arts in Swahili program there. Roughly 2% of people from Njombe ever finish a university degree. Her goal is to get a PhD and then to bring it back to the region. Her entire 18-month master's program (tuition, registration, fees, books, supplies) comes to 3,060,000 TSh, about $1,161. Since this worked out, I kept adding students as I could afford to, and in 2021 I registered it as a 501(c)(3), the Tanzania Education Project. It supports five students from Ibumila now, school fees and healthcare. I kept it small while I was finishing my PhD because I didn't want commitments I couldn't personally guarantee for a decade; I've since started a postdoc, so it feels like the right time to grow past my own paycheck. The long-term goal is that every kid in the village has access to education and healthcare. I sometimes think of this project as a slow experiment. How much could the village itself change over someone's lifetime if the kids have access to education? https://tanzaniaeducationproject.org/ is the website. Nobody takes a salary, and aside from bank fees the money goes to the students. If anyone wants to fund Anwarite's master's specifically, it's here: https://www.gofundme.com/f/send-anwarite-to-her-masters-prog... Happy to answer any questions or take any tips you all might have about doing this sort of thing.

leads.title: I posted 100 tiktoks as introverted engineer
leads.description: I've been coding for over 10 years. I've been employed in a corporation, startup... Then I opened my own startup, raised money, struggled, closed it. This year I wanted to ride a wave of solo builders (inspired by Pieter Levels, Marc Lou and others). It sounded awesome, and I hate to admit, but it sounded kinda easy. Build an app in a week, find viral formats on TikTok, recreate them, go viral, get rich. Easy right? Well. I have locked my introvert personality in a box and put it under my bed, while I started filming my self to promote my apps. First few videos got 700 views... well you gotta start somewhere right? But then I just didn't manage to escape that prison. Somewhere in between I actually managed to get first customers; around $150... nothing mind blowing, I know. After 60 posted videos I started doubting everything... and the obvious happened. I have started building a new app. I just wanted to feel productive again... It worked!.. for a day or two. Then again the distribution time has came.. Same rabbit hole. Posting on Reddit was another idea, but I know it's likely in exchange for my soul (bad experience launching software there :)). Not sure if I even want to ask anything or just share my story at this point... But if there is anyone who reads this and thinks: "Damn I am complete opposite, I love filming videos and marketing, but don't have ideas or can't build." Make sure to contact me :D

leads.title: Calculation of CRC7
leads.description: For a SD card driver I tried to calculate CRC7 for the commands. Now, if I "enable CRC7 check" with CMD59, I get errors with some SD cards. But if I "disable CRC7" check with CMD59, I can read and write files on all kinds of SD cards, who support SPI. Well, my initial assumption was that it was due to the CRC7 calculation. With SD cards that give me errors, I can still initialize them without any problems with "enabled CRC7 check" and also read and write a few files. But usually only about 10-15 files at most before an error occurs. The error manifests itself as follows: After CMD17, I get R1 = 0x00. But then I only read 0xFF. The data token never comes. Also no Data Error Token. Only 0xFF. I read 100 times (100 bytes), but at least for 200 ms (the SD card standard specifies that a timeout can be assumed after 100 ms, so I should be on the safe side to not miss the token). But I only get 0xFF. When I read the status again with CMD13, I get R1 = 0x00 and R2 = 0x00. So no error. From this point on, neither writing nor reading works. I can execute all commands without errors in R1 or R2 (also CMD17,18,24,25), but I only get 0xFF when reading afterwards; the tokens never come. But always with no indication of errors. If someone is interested, the SD card initialization process is done like this: baudrate <400'000 Hz CMD0 -> CMD59 -> CMD8 IF SDSC: CMD58 -> loop(CMD55 -> ACMD41) IF SDHC/SDXC:CMD58 (get OCR register values) -> loop(CMD55 -> ACMD41) -> CDMD50 (get OCR register values and check CCS) CMD9 -> Check CSD-Version and get values CMD10 (get CID register values) CMD55 -> ACMD13 (get SD register values) CMD55 -> ACDM51 (get SCR register values) check, if CMD42 is supported if yes and password should be set or is set: CMD16 (set block length for CMD42) CMD42 CMD16 (set block length 51 bytes, for all card) Mount filesystem Switch to baudrate 12 MHz Read with CMD17, CMD18 (CMD12 for STOP_TRAN) Write with CMD24, CMD25 if error, check with CDM13 I would now like to rule out that it is due to the CRC7 calculation, which may only return an error with certain inputs. Here is the code (Python/Micropython), and I would be grateful if someone familiar with CRC could check it for correctness. As I said, without CRC7 check, I never get an error, but with CRC7 check, until a error arrives, all CRC7 are calculated correct (double checked with CRC-Calculator ) def crc7(self, cmd, arg1, arg2, arg3, arg4): crc = 0x00 poly = 0x89 cmd_token = bytes([cmd, arg1, arg2, arg3, arg4]) # Example: CMD0 -> 0x40, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00 for byte in cmd_token: for bit in range(8): bit = ((byte >> (7 - bit)) & 1) crc_bit = ((crc >> 6) & 1) crc = ((crc << 1) & 0x7F) if bit ^ crc_bit: crc ^= poly crc = crc & 0x7F crc = (crc << 1) | 0x01 # CRC7 and end bit = 1 for CMD return crc

leads.description: I am trying to implement cross-validation with PyTorch; I am used to Sklearn's cross_validation function which is much simpler to use (most likely because I did not fully understand what was happening under the hood); I was hoping someone could advise if first of all this looks correct and, if it does, if there is a better way to write this. I have looked at other posts, and got inspiration from there but I could not find exactly what I am trying to create, which is: Loop through the dataset for n_splits (in my case 5). On each loop, train the model on the train split. Evaluate the model on the test split. Calculate the RMSE of the model evaluation on the test split. At the end of the 5 folds, return the average RMSE of the 5 folds. And as I was creating this, I have started wondering: how should one decide the number of epochs for cross-validation? I always assumed that this would just be 1 but from what I saw in other posts this number can actually vary. Here is my code: X = main_df.drop(columns=['target']) y = main_df['target'] X_train_t = torch.tensor(X.values, dtype=torch.float32) y_train_t = torch.tensor(y.values, dtype=torch.float32) cv_dataset = TensorDataset(X_train_t, y_train_t) class NetModel(nn.Module): def __init__(self, in_count): super(NetModel, self).__init__() self.layers = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(in_count, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 1) ) def forward(self, x): out = self.layers(x) return out num_epochs = 1 kfold = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) tot_rmse = 0.0 for fold, (train_ids, test_ids) in enumerate(kfold.split(cv_dataset)): print(f'FOLD {fold+1}') train_subsampler = torch.utils.data.SubsetRandomSampler(train_ids) test_subsampler = torch.utils.data.SubsetRandomSampler(test_ids) train_loader = DataLoader(cv_dataset, batch_size=5, sampler=train_subsampler) test_loader = DataLoader(cv_dataset, batch_size=5, sampler=test_subsampler) # initialize model model = NetModel(X_train_t.shape[1]) criterion = nn.MSELoss() optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.0001) for epoch in range(num_epochs): current_loss = 0.0 model.train() for i, data in enumerate(train_loader, 0): inputs, targets = data targets = targets.reshape((targets.shape[0], 1)) optimizer.zero_grad() outputs = model(inputs) loss = criterion(outputs, targets) loss.backward() optimizer.step() fold_rmse = 0.0 model.eval() with torch.no_grad(): for i, data in enumerate(test_loader, 0): inputs, targets = data targets = targets.reshape((targets.shape[0], 1)) outputs = model(inputs) rmse = root_mean_squared_error(targets, outputs) # accumulate rmse of the fold fold_rmse += rmse print(f"Sum of fold {fold+1} RMSE: {fold_rmse:.3f} | Count batches: {i+1}") # calculate average of the fold rmse (accumulated rmse / number of batches) tot_rmse += fold_rmse/(i+1) print("--------------------------------------------------") print(f"Avg. RMSE: {tot_rmse/5}") This is the output of the above: FOLD 1 Sum of fold 1 RMSE: 2124.690 | Count batches: 89 -------------------------------------------------- FOLD 2 Sum of fold 2 RMSE: 1817.517 | Count batches: 89 -------------------------------------------------- FOLD 3 Sum of fold 3 RMSE: 2160.074 | Count batches: 89 -------------------------------------------------- FOLD 4 Sum of fold 4 RMSE: 1613.786 | Count batches: 89 -------------------------------------------------- FOLD 5 Sum of fold 5 RMSE: 1713.522 | Count batches: 89 -------------------------------------------------- Avg. leads.description: I am a JAX beginner and someone experienced with JAX told me that if we have repeated calls to a scan / for loop (e.g. when these are themselves wrapped by another for loop), it might be better to leave the loop as a for instead of converting it to a scan because the for loop is unrolled completely and only has the 1-time huge compilation cost while the scan is not unrolled by default and even though its compilation cost will be small, the fact that it is rolled will mean that the cost of repeatedly running this loop will end up making the scan more expensive than the for . This did not strike me immediately when I started writing my code, but made sense upon thinking about it. So, I tested this assumption using code based on the following pseudo-code (the full code is really long and I hope these relevant parts I provide here are easier to understand): for i in range(num_train_steps): # Currently fixed to be a for loop for j in range(num_env_steps): # Currently fixed to be a for loop act() def act(): for k in range(num_algo_iters): # Currently playing around with making this one either a scan or a for loop jax.lax.scan(rollout_func) # Currently fixed to be a scan The only loop in the above code that I tested switching between scan and for was the k loop and then I varied the variable num_env_steps to be 1, 100, 1000 and 10000 to see whether increasing the number of times the act() (and thus the k loop) was executed made a difference to the timing. (The testing was done with 5 iterations for the k for loop and 2 iterations for the innermost scan although these are variable in general, if that matters.) The times taken for act() for the different repeats were 1.5, 11.3,, 99.0, 956.2 seconds for the scan version and 5.1, 14.5, 103.6, 972.7 seconds for the for version. So the for version never ended up faster for the number of repeats I tried. So, now I am wondering if for any number of repeats (i.e. num_env_steps ), the unrolling of the for actually makes the program faster than with scan . My questions: Would maybe increasing the repeats even more by setting num_env_steps to 100k or 1 million make it faster or can we always just replace a for with a scan ? I have this question because I wonder if I am trying to over-optimise my code by converting every for to a scan . If I set unroll = True for the scan , would it then always be fine to replace all for s with scan s and expect speed-ups? Is there a rule of thumb that can help me decide when to use for and when to use scan if I am only interested in such speed-ups? act was jitted by the way.

leads.title: __await__: may it be called several times and then wait again?
leads.description: For iterators, there is a clear protocol: once they are exhausted, they remain exhausted. It is not allowed to create an iterator whose __next__() raises StopIteration and, called once again, return a value again. My question: is there a similar protocol/contract for __await__ ? Whenever I see a class whose objects can be awaited on, they either can only be __await__ ed once at all (e. g. coroutines) or always provide the same value again (but once the value is there, they don't "block" again (in the async sense - I don't know whether that's the right word for that, it isn't really blocking). E. g., a Future , once it has a result, provides this result on await future , but never can lose that. or have a method which provides the __await__ . E. g., Event.wait() . An Event can be set and reset, but await ing on it happens via this method. I am planning to create a class which provides a value by await ing on its objects, but "block" (again, in the async sense) once it hasn't one. But I wonder why there is a kind of contract similar to the one mentionned above for iterators. Could the Event have been designed in a way that I can directly await on the object instead of it having a method? I am asking because I am planning to create a thing I am about to call SignalManager . It is a context manager which installs signal handlers on entering and deinstall them on exiting. While it is active, I can (in a loop or in a Task) await signals in order to capture get the next signal and "do something with it".
